paragraphs.text: Meta has built a humanoid robot prototype called Max together with Fourier, a robotics company based in Shanghai, according to a report by The Information published on October 31, 2026, and summarized by PYMNTS. The report cited people familiar with the project. Neither company has published an announcement or official specifications.
The work is aimed at robots that could one day handle chores and other everyday tasks in the home, PYMNTS reported. Meta told the outlets it has no plans to sell the units it built with Fourier.
What the Max prototype can do

According to the report, Max stands about 5 feet tall, has speakers built into its chest and a face that can mimic human expressions. Its five-fingered hands can pick up small objects. The robot can recognize a voice, interpret a hand gesture and signal when it is listening or thinking.

The first prototype reportedly took about three months to build. A second version, described in the report as Max 2, is already in development. PYMNTS said it adds better manipulation skills, a projector for showing visual content and sensors that help it walk up and down steps.
No launch target has been set, according to PYMNTS. The prototypes are meant to help Meta develop a robot it could eventually sell, even though the Fourier units themselves are not for sale.
Why Meta is working with a Chinese partner

A Meta spokesperson said the company faces the same sourcing challenges as the rest of the industry for components that are not readily available in the United States. The spokesperson described the Fourier effort as focused on internal research and experimentation.

The partnership comes as restrictions grow on American companies doing business with Chinese firms, PYMNTS noted. Reuters picked up the original report but said it could not immediately verify it, according to ShiftDelete.Net.

Fourier was founded in 2015 and began by making rehabilitation exoskeletons. It unveiled its first general-purpose humanoid, the GR-1, in 2023 and has since released newer GR-series robots aimed at care and assistance. Its GR-3, a care-focused humanoid about 165 centimeters tall, made its United States debut at CES in January 2026.

Meta's interest in humanoids is not new. In a February 2025 internal memo cited by ShiftDelete.Net, Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth wrote that the robotics group would focus on consumer humanoid robots that would maximize the capabilities of Meta's Llama platform.

Meta has also acquired Assured Robot Intelligence, a startup developing AI models for humanoid robots, PYMNTS reported in May. According to PYMNTS, the company hopes its robotics work can build on the success of its AI agent, Muse.

Taken together, the reports describe a company that wants to own the software brain of a home robot while borrowing hardware experience from a partner that already ships humanoids. Building a working prototype in about three months suggests Meta is moving quickly, but a research robot and a product people can buy are very different things. Safety, price and supply chains all stand between the two, and the China link adds a political question that a purely domestic build would avoid.
The next signal to watch is whether Meta shows Max or Max 2 publicly, or names a supplier for a robot it actually intends to sell.
